facts.fact: Name for the term: "lưu vực" (used for the Rio Negro basin in Brazil: "lưu vực Rio Negro")
In fishkeeping, a drainage basin or river system matters as the geographic unit a biotope aquarium copies: fish, plants and decor all come from one place in nature, such as the Amazon River.
One river system can hold many separate biotopes, so a whole river system is not one single habitat.
Species from different tributaries of the same river system may never meet in the wild, so the guide advises researching the exact collection locality where possible.

Aquarium Care sorts biotopes into three levels. Biotope A recreates one exact area. Biotope B allows species from the same habitat type. Biotope C allows species from different areas as long as they share environmental conditions.
Habitat factors to copy include pH, water hardness, organic and inorganic content, flow speed and temperature.
An Amazon biotope tank (Aquarium Care) suggests 24-30 °C, pH 6 to 7 and 2 to 10 dH hardness.
A Mekong River biotope guide gives 24–28 °C, pH 6.5–7.5 and GH 5–15 dGH, calling the water relatively neutral and adaptable.
Example of a basin mismatch: Neon Tetra (South America) does not belong in a biotope tank copying the Mekong River (Southeast Asia).
Step 1: choose the habitat or region first, because it decides everything else.
Step 2: research the region's water chemistry, substrate, typical plants and seasonal conditions before buying anything.
Step 3: pick the tank size (60-80 litres suggested for a first biotope) and check that the floor can bear the weight.
Step 4: match the substrate and hardscape to the habitat.
Step 5: stock only species that live together in that habitat, and only plants native to the region, or no plants if the habitat is naturally bare.
Step 6: adjust the water to the target biotope before adding fish, and test pH, GH and KH weekly while cycling.
Step 7: cycle the tank for four to six weeks, then add livestock gradually, starting with the hardiest species.
For a Mekong River biotope, use a tank of 120 cm or larger, fine river sand with smooth pebbles and cobbles, and moderate to strong flow from a powerhead at one end.
Plants suggested for a Mekong biotope: Cryptocoryne along calm edges, Vallisneria in sand with moderate current, Hygrophila, and Crinum natans or C. calamistratum.
Use only fish, shrimp, snails and plants that come from the biotope you researched.
Use only fish and plants from the same ecological region ("Chỉ sử dụng loài cá và cây cùng vùng sinh thái").
Mixing fish from different continents or habitats in one biotope.
Assuming all fish from one habitat get along: some species from the same habitat are not suitable tankmates. Peacock bass, for example, eat small tetras, their natural food in the wild.
Stocking species that do not share a habitat in nature, or adding plants to a habitat that is naturally plant-free.
Overlooking the weight: an 80-litre biotope setup can weigh roughly 100 kg.
Overusing moss or plants from outside the original ecological region ("Không lạm dụng rêu hoặc cây ngoài vùng sinh thái gốc").
Adding fish before cycling, which can cause shock and death from high ammonia/nitrite.
Buying fish and plants from unclear sources, which can bring disease or the wrong species.
A Mekong River biotope guide lists clown loach (Chromobotia macracanthus) among Mekong fish.
Chromobotia macracanthus is endemic to Indonesia (Sumatra and Borneo).
Clown loach (Chromobotia macracanthus) needs 300+ litres and grows to 30 cm. Bala shark (Balantiocheilos melanopterus) reaches 30 cm and suits only very large setups.
aquariumscience.org says the idea that fish from different pH, GH or KH waters cannot be mixed is a myth, and argues water parameters matter little when mixing biotopes.
aquariumscience.org calls the rule that American and African cichlids cannot be kept together one that is often broken successfully.
aquariumscience.org advises against mixing fish when the smallest is less than half the length of the largest.
The lower Mekong flows through Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam.
A Southeast Asian biotope usually copies rivers, streams or flooded forests in Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia or Indonesia, for example a stream in Vietnam.
Bucep Việt describes a Vietnam Stream Biotope: a mountain stream with moss, rocks and decaying leaves. It lists "cá bống suối, cá trâm, tép Yamato, ốc táo vàng" without scientific names.
Setting up biotope tanks is described as a trend favoured by fishkeepers in Vietnam, with Southeast Asian, Amazon and rock-stream styles common.
Aquatech notes Anubias is used in Southeast Asian biotopes even though Anubias is of African origin.
